entry.sum: Homological algebra starts from exact sequences and the functors that preserve them only in part: $\mathrm{Hom}$ is left exact and $\otimes$ right exact, and the modules on which they are exact are the projective, injective and flat ones. The snake and five lemmas, valid in any abelian category, turn short exact sequences of complexes into long exact homology sequences, and projective or injective resolutions, unique up to chain homotopy by the comparison theorem, prepare the ground for derived functors.
key: 0\to A\to B\to C\to 0 \ \Longrightarrow\ 0\to\mathrm{Hom}(M,A)\to\mathrm{Hom}(M,B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(M,C),\quad M\otimes A\to M\otimes B\to M\otimes C\to 0
entry.why: Papers in algebra, topology and representation theory chase elements through diagrams of exact sequences in whatever abelian category they work in, and every derived functor (Ext, Tor, sheaf and group cohomology) is computed from the projective or injective resolutions built here.

links.note: Representations of a poset (persistence modules) form an abelian category, and exact structures on it are chosen to define homological invariants.
Sheaves of abelian groups form an abelian category with enough injectives, so the diagram lemmas and injective resolutions of this page apply to them.

blocks.body:
Multiplication by $2$ is an injective map $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$. Tensor it with $\mathbb{Z}/2$ and it becomes the zero map $\mathbb{Z}/2\to\mathbb{Z}/2$, which is not injective. Apply $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb{Z}/2)$ instead and the result is again zero, now failing to be surjective. Which maps stay injective or surjective when a functor is applied is a question about exact sequences, and this page develops the language and the tools for it: exact sequences in abelian categories, the exactness properties of $\mathrm{Hom}$ and $\otimes$ and the modules (projective, injective, flat) on which they are exact, the snake and five lemmas, chain complexes and the long exact homology sequence, splicing, and projective and injective resolutions with the comparison theorem and the horseshoe lemma.

Research papers use this material in two ways. They chase elements through diagrams of exact sequences in whatever abelian category they work in: persistence modules for Blanchette-Brüstle-Hanson, inverse systems for Bannister, homotopy groups of spectra for the Smith fiber sequence paper. And they replace a module by a resolution in order to define derived functors; that second use is the subject of [[derived-functors]], and of [[tor]] and [[ext]], which are built on it. The page uses the language of [[modules]] (with the structure theorem over a PID) and [[categories-functors]] (functors, natural transformations, adjunctions), and the chain complexes of [[homology]]. Rings are associative with $1$; when a statement needs $R$ commutative, it says so.

blocks.title: Exact sequences and abelian categories
blocks.body:
A sequence of module homomorphisms $\cdots\to M_{i-1}\xrightarrow{f_{i-1}} M_i\xrightarrow{f_i} M_{i+1}\to\cdots$ is exact at $M_i$ if $\operatorname{im} f_{i-1} = \ker f_i$, and exact if it is exact at every inner term. This is the same condition that appeared in the Mayer-Vietoris sequence on the [[homology]] page. Three special cases carry most of the information.

1. $0\to A\xrightarrow{f} B$ is exact exactly when $f$ is injective, and $B\xrightarrow{g} C\to 0$ is exact exactly when $g$ is surjective.
2. A short exact sequence $0\to A\xrightarrow{f} B\xrightarrow{g} C\to 0$ says that $f$ identifies $A$ with a submodule of $B$ and $g$ identifies $C$ with the quotient $B/f(A)$. One also says that $B$ is an extension of $C$ by $A$.
3. A long exact sequence breaks into short ones: if $\cdots\to M_{i-1}\to M_i\to M_{i+1}\to\cdots$ is exact, then $0\to \ker f_i\to M_i\to \ker f_{i+1}\to 0$ is short exact, because $\operatorname{im} f_i = \ker f_{i+1}$.

The definitions use only kernels, images and cokernels, so they make sense in any category where those exist and behave as they do for modules. Such a category is called abelian. The Stacks Project gives the shortest form of the definition: an additive category (Hom sets are abelian groups, composition is bilinear, finite direct sums exist) in which every morphism has a kernel and a cokernel, and in which the canonical map from the coimage $\operatorname{Coker}(\ker f\to X)$ to the image $\operatorname{Ker}(Y\to\operatorname{coker} f)$ is an isomorphism. Arapura lists the same conditions as seven axioms A1-A7 and gives examples and non-examples: $R$-modules, and finitely generated modules over a left Noetherian ring, form abelian categories; free abelian groups form an additive category that is not abelian (the cokernel of $2\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ taken in abelian groups, $\mathbb{Z}/2$, is not free, and inside free groups this map has zero kernel and zero cokernel without being an isomorphism), and Hausdorff topological abelian groups fail the last axiom (a continuous bijection need not be a homeomorphism). Other abelian categories met in the papers below are chain complexes, sheaves of abelian groups, and representations of a poset (persistence modules).

In an abelian category, objects need not have elements, yet textbook proofs chase elements through diagrams. The Freyd-Mitchell embedding theorem (Arapura's Theorem 5.8, Weibel's 1.6.1) justifies this: a small abelian category admits a fully faithful exact functor into a category of modules. Every diagram lemma that involves finitely many objects therefore holds in an abelian category as soon as it holds for modules (one first passes to the small abelian subcategory generated by the diagram). In practice, papers state such lemmas for modules and use them freely in any abelian category.

blocks.title: Split exact sequence
blocks.body:
A short exact sequence $0\to A\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{g}C\to 0$ is split if it is isomorphic to $0\to A\to A\oplus C\to C\to 0$ (inclusion and projection) by an isomorphism $B\cong A\oplus C$ that is the identity on $A$ and on $C$. Equivalently (the splitting lemma):

1. there is $r\colon B\to A$ with $rf = \mathrm{id}_A$ (a retraction), or
2. there is $s\colon C\to B$ with $gs = \mathrm{id}_C$ (a section).

Given $r$, the map $B\to A\oplus C$, $b\mapsto (r(b), g(b))$ is an isomorphism; given $s$, the map $A\oplus C\to B$, $(a,c)\mapsto f(a)+s(c)$ is one. Checking these two claims is a short element chase that is worth doing once.

blocks.title: Exact sequences that do not split
blocks.body: Show that $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/n\to0$ $(n\ge 2)$ and $0\to\mathbb{Z}/2\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}/4\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$ are exact and not split, while $0\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to\mathbb{Z}/6\to\mathbb{Z}/3\to0$ (first map $x\mapsto 3x$) is split.
blocks.solution:
In the first sequence multiplication by $n$ is injective, its image $n\mathbb{Z}$ is the kernel of reduction mod $n$, and reduction is onto. A section $s\colon\mathbb{Z}/n\to\mathbb{Z}$ would send the element $1$ of order $n$ to an element of finite order in $\mathbb{Z}$, hence to $0$, so $gs = 0\ne\mathrm{id}$. No splitting.

In the second, $x\mapsto 2x$ sends $\mathbb{Z}/2$ onto $\{0,2\}\subset\mathbb{Z}/4$, the kernel of reduction mod $2$. A splitting would give $\mathbb{Z}/4\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2$, impossible since $\mathbb{Z}/4$ has an element of order $4$.

In the third, $x\mapsto 3x$ embeds $\mathbb{Z}/2$ as $\{0,3\}$, the kernel of reduction mod $3$. The map $s\colon\mathbb{Z}/3\to\mathbb{Z}/6$, $s(y) = 4y$ is well defined ($4\cdot3 = 12\equiv0$) and $4y\equiv y \pmod 3$, so $gs = \mathrm{id}$: the sequence splits, matching $\mathbb{Z}/6\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3$ from the [[modules]] page. The non-split examples will reappear as the non-zero elements of $\mathrm{Ext}^1$.

blocks.body:
1. Prove the splitting lemma: show that a retraction $r$ exists if and only if a section $s$ exists, and that either gives $B\cong A\oplus C$ compatibly with $f$ and $g$.
2. Show that every short exact sequence of vector spaces splits, and that $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ with $C$ free splits for modules over any ring.
3. Let $0\to M_1\to M_2\to\cdots\to M_k\to 0$ be exact with all $M_i$ finite. Show that $\prod_i |M_i|^{(-1)^i} = 1$. (Break into short exact sequences.)
4. Show that the category of finite abelian groups is abelian, and that the category of finitely generated free abelian groups is additive but not abelian.

blocks.title: Exactness of Hom and tensor; projective, injective and flat modules
blocks.body:
A functor between abelian categories is additive if it is additive on Hom groups; additive functors preserve finite direct sums and hence split exact sequences. An additive covariant functor $F$ is exact if it sends short exact sequences to short exact sequences, left exact if $0\to A\to B\to C\to 0$ exact implies $0\to FA\to FB\to FC$ exact, and right exact if it implies $FA\to FB\to FC\to0$ exact. For a contravariant functor the arrows reverse: $\mathrm{Hom}(-,N)$ is left exact means $0\to\mathrm{Hom}(C,N)\to\mathrm{Hom}(B,N)\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,N)$ is exact.

The basic facts, for modules over a ring $R$ and a short exact sequence $0\to A\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{g}C\to0$:

1. $\mathrm{Hom}_R(M,-)$ is left exact (covariant).
2. $\mathrm{Hom}_R(-,N)$ is left exact (contravariant).
3. $-\otimes_R M$ is right exact.

None of the three is exact in general, and the examples in the introduction show it: $2\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ is injective, $\mathbb{Z}/2\otimes 2 = 0$ is not, and $\mathrm{Hom}(2,\mathbb{Z}/2) = 0$ is not surjective. Likewise $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/2,-)$ applied to $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/2$ gives $0\to\mathbb{Z}/2$, not surjective.

The modules on which these functors are exact get names. A module $P$ is projective if $\mathrm{Hom}(P,-)$ is exact, injective if $\mathrm{Hom}(-,I)$ is exact, and flat if $-\otimes F$ is exact. Since the functors are left (or right) exact anyway, the conditions say: every surjection $B\to C$ induces a surjection $\mathrm{Hom}(P,B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(P,C)$, so maps out of $P$ lift along surjections; every injection $A\to B$ induces a surjection $\mathrm{Hom}(B,I)\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,I)$, so maps into $I$ extend along injections; and $-\otimes F$ preserves injections. Free modules are projective (send each basis element to any preimage), and a module is projective if and only if it is a direct summand of a free module, by applying the lifting property to a surjection from a free module onto $P$ and the splitting lemma. Projective modules are flat, because $-\otimes R^{(I)}$ is a direct sum of copies of the identity and summands of exact functors are exact. The converse fails: $\mathbb{Q}$ is a flat $\mathbb{Z}$-module (it is a localisation of $\mathbb{Z}$) but not projective, since it is not a summand of a free abelian group (a free abelian group has no non-zero element divisible by every integer).

blocks.title: Left exactness of Hom, right exactness of tensor
blocks.body:
Let $0\to A\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{g}C\to0$ be exact. Then for every module $M$ (left modules, with $M$ a right module for the tensor product)
$$\begin{aligned}&0\to\mathrm{Hom}(M,A)\xrightarrow{f_*}\mathrm{Hom}(M,B)\xrightarrow{g_*}{}\\ &\qquad\mathrm{Hom}(M,C),\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}&0\to\mathrm{Hom}(C,M)\xrightarrow{g^*}\mathrm{Hom}(B,M)\xrightarrow{f^*}{}\\ &\qquad\mathrm{Hom}(A,M),\end{aligned}$$
$$M\otimes A\to M\otimes B\to M\otimes C\to 0$$
are exact.

First sequence. If $f\circ u = 0$ then $u = 0$ because $f$ is injective. Clearly $g_*f_* = (gf)_* = 0$. If $g\circ v = 0$ for $v\colon M\to B$, then $v(M)\subseteq\ker g = f(A)$, and $u = f^{-1}\circ v$ is a homomorphism $M\to A$ with $f_*u = v$.

Second sequence. If $\varphi\circ g = 0$ then $\varphi = 0$ since $g$ is onto. $f^*g^* = (gf)^* = 0$. If $\psi\colon B\to M$ vanishes on $f(A) = \ker g$, it factors through $B/\ker g\cong C$, i.e. $\psi = \varphi\circ g$.

Third sequence. Surjectivity of $M\otimes B\to M\otimes C$ holds because the elements $m\otimes c = m\otimes g(b)$ generate. The composite is $M\otimes gf = 0$, so $1\otimes g$ factors through $Q = (M\otimes B)/\operatorname{im}(1\otimes f)$, giving $\bar g\colon Q\to M\otimes C$; we show $\bar g$ is an isomorphism. Define $M\times C\to Q$ by $(m,c)\mapsto [m\otimes b]$ for any $b$ with $g(b) = c$. This is well defined: two choices differ by $f(a)$, and $m\otimes f(a)\in\operatorname{im}(1\otimes f)$. It is bilinear, so it induces $M\otimes C\to Q$, which is inverse to $\bar g$ on generators. Hence $\ker(1\otimes g) = \operatorname{im}(1\otimes f)$.

(Alternatively, the third statement follows from the second and the adjunction $\mathrm{Hom}(M\otimes B, N)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(B,\mathrm{Hom}(M,N))$ of [[categories-functors]]: a sequence $X\to Y\to Z\to 0$ is exact as soon as
$$\begin{aligned}&0\to\mathrm{Hom}(Z,N)\to\mathrm{Hom}(Y,N)\to{}\\ &\qquad\mathrm{Hom}(X,N)\end{aligned}$$
is exact for every $N$. This is the general principle that left adjoints are right exact.)

blocks.title: Four descriptions of projective modules
blocks.body: Projectivity is the hypothesis behind every resolution on this page. The sources characterise it in different, equivalent ways.

items.label: Lifting property
items.body: $P$ is projective when every map $P\to C$ lifts through every surjection $B\to C$. This is the definition that drives the comparison theorem: maps out of a projective can always be pushed back along an epimorphism.

items.label: Summand of free
items.body: Over a ring, $P$ is projective exactly when $P\oplus Q\cong R^{(I)}$ for some $Q$ and some free module. So projectives are 'free up to a complement'; finitely generated projectives over a commutative local ring are free (Weibel, Proposition 4.3.11), and over a PID projectives are free because submodules of free modules are.

items.label: Splitting
items.body: $P$ is projective exactly when every short exact sequence $0\to A\to B\to P\to0$ splits. This makes projectivity a statement about extensions, and in the language of [[ext]], about the vanishing of $\mathrm{Ext}^1(P,-)$.

items.label: Vanishing of Ext
items.body: Once Ext is available ([[ext]]): $P$ is projective if and only if $\mathrm{Ext}^1(P,M) = 0$ for all $M$, if and only if $\mathrm{Ext}^i(P,M) = 0$ for all $i>0$ and all $M$. Papers in representation theory and commutative algebra typically use this form, and a footnote in Blanchette-Brüstle-Hanson quotes it as the way projectives are recognised.

blocks.title: Baer's criterion and divisible groups
blocks.body:
1. (Baer) A left $R$-module $E$ is injective if and only if for every left ideal $J\subseteq R$, every homomorphism $J\to E$ extends to a homomorphism $R\to E$.
2. Over a principal ideal domain $R$, a module $E$ is injective if and only if it is divisible: for every $e\in E$ and every non-zero $r\in R$ there is $x\in E$ with $rx = e$. In particular $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ and the Prüfer groups $\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty) = \mathbb{Z}[1/p]/\mathbb{Z}$ are injective $\mathbb{Z}$-modules, while $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}/n$ $(n\ge2)$ are not.

1. Necessity is the definition applied to $J\hookrightarrow R$. For sufficiency, let $A\subseteq B$ and $\varphi\colon A	o E$. Consider pairs $(A',\varphi')$ with $A\subseteq A'\subseteq B$ and $\varphi'$ extending $\varphi$, ordered by extension. A chain has an upper bound (the union), so by Zorn's lemma there is a maximal pair $(A',\varphi')$. Suppose $A'
eq B$ and pick $b\in B\setminus A'$. Let $J = \{r\in R: rb\in A'\}$, a left ideal, and define $\psi\colon J	o E$, $\psi(r) = \varphi'(rb)$. By hypothesis $\psi$ extends to $R$; let $e = \psi(1)$ for the extension. Define $\varphi''$ on $A'+Rb$ by $\varphi''(a+rb) = \varphi'(a)+re$. It is well defined: if $a+rb = a'+r'b$ then $(r-r')b = a'-a\in A'$, so $r-r'\in J$ and $\varphi'(a'-a) = \psi(r-r') = (r-r')e$. This extends $\varphi'$ strictly, contradicting maximality. So $A' = B$.

2. Let $R$ be a PID. If $E$ is injective, $e\in E$ and $r
eq0$, the map $Rr	o E$, $sr\mapsto se$, is well defined because $R$ is a domain; extending it to $R$ and evaluating at $1$ gives $x$ with $rx = e$. Conversely, if $E$ is divisible, every ideal is $J = Rr$; a map $\varphi\colon Rr	o E$ is determined by $e = \varphi(r)$, and for $r
eq 0$ choose $x$ with $rx = e$; then $s\mapsto sx$ extends $\varphi$ (the case $r = 0$ is trivial). Baer's criterion finishes. The listed groups are visibly divisible; $\mathbb{Z}$ is not ($1 = 2x$ has no solution), and in $\mathbb{Z}/n$ the element $1$ is not divisible by $n$.

blocks.title: Enough projectives and enough injectives
blocks.body:
An abelian category has enough projectives if every object is a quotient of a projective one, and enough injectives if every object embeds in an injective one. Module categories have enough projectives: the free module on the elements of $M$ maps onto $M$. They also have enough injectives, and this is the less obvious fact. For abelian groups: write $M = \mathbb{Z}^{(I)}/K$; then $M$ embeds in $\mathbb{Q}^{(I)}/K$, which is divisible, hence injective. For $R$-modules, one uses the coinduced module $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(R,D)$ for a divisible group $D$, which is an injective $R$-module because of the adjunction
$$\mathrm{Hom}_R(N,\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(R,D))\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(N,D),$$
whose right-hand side is exact in $N$. The underlying principle (Weibel's Proposition 2.3.10, used in Bannister's paper on derived limits in his Lemma 3.22) is: if $L\dashv G$ is an adjunction and the left adjoint $L$ is exact, then the right adjoint $G$ preserves injective objects, since $\mathrm{Hom}(-,GI)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(L(-),I)$ is a composite of exact functors.

Not every abelian category has enough of both. Arapura notes (his Example 5.12) that finitely generated abelian groups do not have enough injectives. In fact that category has no non-zero injective objects: extending maps along $n\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ shows that an injective object there is divisible, and a non-zero finitely generated group never is. Which kind of resolution exists decides which definition of a derived functor is available, and this is why Tang's paper on condensed and profinite modules has to discuss which resolutions are available before it can compare Ext groups.

blocks.title: Testing projective, injective and flat
blocks.body: Decide which of the $\mathbb{Z}$-modules $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Z}/6$, $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ are projective, injective or flat; then decide the same for the module $\mathbb{Z}/2$ over the ring $\mathbb{Z}/6$ and over the ring $\mathbb{Z}/4$.
blocks.solution:
Over $\mathbb{Z}$: projective means free (subgroups of free abelian groups are free, by the [[modules]] page), injective means divisible, and flat means torsion-free (shown on the [[tor]] page). So $\mathbb{Z}$ is projective and flat, not injective. $\mathbb{Z}/6$ is none of the three. $\mathbb{Q}$ is flat and injective, not projective. $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is injective, not flat (it has torsion) and not projective.

Over $\mathbb{Z}/6$: by the Chinese remainder theorem $\mathbb{Z}/6\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\times\mathbb{Z}/3$ as rings, and $\mathbb{Z}/2$ is the direct summand $\{0,3\}$ of the free module $\mathbb{Z}/6$. So it is projective, hence flat; it is also injective, by Baer's criterion: the ideals of $\mathbb{Z}/6$ are $0$, $(2)$, $(3)$, $(1)$, and a map from $(3) = \{0,3\}$ or $(2) = \{0,2,4\}$ to $\mathbb{Z}/2$ extends (for $(2)$ the only map is $0$ since $(2)$ has order $3$; for $(3)$, $3\mapsto 1$ extends by $1\mapsto 1$).

Over $\mathbb{Z}/4$: $\mathbb{Z}/2$ is not a summand of a free $\mathbb{Z}/4$-module. Suppose it were a summand of $(\mathbb{Z}/4)^n$, with projection $\pi$ onto it, and let $e$ be its generator. Every element of order $2$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/4)^n$ has all coordinates in $\{0,2\}$, so $e = 2y$ for some $y$; then $e = \pi(e) = 2\pi(y) = 0$, because $2$ kills $\mathbb{Z}/2$. Contradiction. Nor is it injective: the map $(2)\to\mathbb{Z}/2$, $2\mapsto 1$ would have to extend to $1\mapsto x$ with $2x = 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}/2$, impossible. And it is not flat: tensoring the injection $\mathbb{Z}/2\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}/4$ with $\mathbb{Z}/2$ over $\mathbb{Z}/4$ gives the zero map $\mathbb{Z}/2\to\mathbb{Z}/2$. The same module can be very well or very badly behaved, depending on the ring.

blocks.body:
1. Show that $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Z}/n,-)$ is not right exact by applying it to $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/n\to0$.
2. Show that a direct sum of projective modules is projective and a product of injective modules is injective.
3. Show that $\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)$ is injective and that every finite abelian $p$-group embeds in a finite direct sum of copies of it.
4. Let $R$ be an integral domain with fraction field $K\ne R$. Show that $K$ is a flat $R$-module that is not projective. (For non-projectivity, imitate the argument for $\mathbb{Q}$ using a non-zero element of a free module.)
5. Prove: if $L\dashv G$ with $L$ exact then $G$ preserves injectives. Deduce that $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(R,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$ is an injective $R$-module.

blocks.title: The snake lemma and the five lemma
blocks.body: Two diagram lemmas do most of the work of homological algebra. The snake lemma manufactures a connecting map from kernels to cokernels; it is the source of every long exact sequence on this page. The five lemma lets one conclude that a map is an isomorphism from information about its neighbours in a ladder of exact sequences; it is how papers such as the Smith fiber sequence paper check that two long exact sequences agree. Both are stated for modules; by Freyd-Mitchell they hold in any abelian category.

blocks.title: Snake lemma
blocks.body:
Consider a commutative diagram of modules with exact rows
$$\begin{array}{ccccccc} & A & \xrightarrow{f} & B & \xrightarrow{g} & C & \to 0\\ & \downarrow\alpha && \downarrow\beta && \downarrow\gamma & \\ 0\to & A' & \xrightarrow{f'} & B' & \xrightarrow{g'} & C' & \end{array}$$
There is a homomorphism $\delta\colon\ker\gamma\to\operatorname{coker}\alpha$ such that
$$\begin{aligned}&\ker\alpha\to\ker\beta\to\ker\gamma\xrightarrow{\delta}{}\\ &\qquad\operatorname{coker}\alpha\to\operatorname{coker}\beta\to\operatorname{coker}\gamma\end{aligned}$$
is exact (Stacks Lemma 12.5.17, Weibel 1.3.2), where the unlabelled maps are induced by $f, g, f', g'$. If moreover $f$ is injective, so is $\ker\alpha\to\ker\beta$; if $g'$ is surjective, so is $\operatorname{coker}\beta\to\operatorname{coker}\gamma$.

blocks.caption: The snake lemma. The kernels sit above and the cokernels below the two exact rows; the connecting map runs from the kernel of the right-hand vertical map to the cokernel of the left-hand one.

0 \arrow[r] & A' \arrow[r, "f'"] \arrow[d] & B' \arrow[r, "g'"] \arrow[d] & C' \arrow[d] & \\
 & \operatorname{coker}\alpha \arrow[r] & \operatorname{coker}\beta \arrow[r] & \operatorname{coker}\gamma &
\end{tikzcd}

blocks.body:
Definition of $\delta$. Let $c\in\ker\gamma$. Choose $b\in B$ with $g(b) = c$. Then $g'\beta(b) = \gamma g(b) = \gamma(c) = 0$, so $\beta(b) = f'(a')$ for a unique $a'\in A'$ ($f'$ is injective). Put $\delta(c) = [a']\in\operatorname{coker}\alpha$. If $b$ is replaced by another preimage $b+f(a)$, then $a'$ changes to $a'+\alpha(a)$, which has the same class. So $\delta$ is well defined, and it is clearly additive.

Exactness at $\ker\beta$. The composite $\ker\alpha\to\ker\beta\to\ker\gamma$ is induced by $gf = 0$. If $b\in\ker\beta$ and $g(b) = 0$, then $b = f(a)$, and $f'\alpha(a) = \beta f(a) = 0$ gives $\alpha(a) = 0$, so $b$ comes from $\ker\alpha$.

Exactness at $\ker\gamma$. If $c = g(b)$ with $b\in\ker\beta$, we may use this $b$ in the definition and get $a' = 0$. Conversely if $\delta(c) = 0$ then $a' = \alpha(a)$ for some $a$, and $b - f(a)$ is a preimage of $c$ with $\beta(b-f(a)) = f'(a')-f'\alpha(a) = 0$, so $c$ comes from $\ker\beta$.

Exactness at $\operatorname{coker}\alpha$. The image of $\delta(c)$ in $\operatorname{coker}\beta$ is $[f'(a')] = [\beta(b)] = 0$. Conversely, if $[f'(a')] = 0$ in $\operatorname{coker}\beta$, then $f'(a') = \beta(b)$ for some $b$; put $c = g(b)$. Then $\gamma(c) = g'\beta(b) = g'f'(a') = 0$, and by construction $\delta(c) = [a']$.

Exactness at $\operatorname{coker}\beta$. The composite is induced by $g'f' = 0$. If $b'\in B'$ maps to $0$ in $\operatorname{coker}\gamma$, then $g'(b') = \gamma(c)$ with $c = g(b)$; so $g'(b'-\beta(b)) = 0$ and $b'-\beta(b) = f'(a')$. Thus $[b'] = [f'(a')]$ is in the image of $\operatorname{coker}\alpha$.

The two addenda are immediate: a restriction of an injective map is injective, and a map induced on quotients by a surjective map is surjective.

blocks.title: Five lemma
blocks.body: Consider a commutative ladder (drawn below) with exact rows $A_1\to A_2\to A_3\to A_4\to A_5$ and $B_1\to B_2\to B_3\to B_4\to B_5$ and vertical maps $\varphi_i\colon A_i\to B_i$ for $i = 1,\dots,5$. If $\varphi_2,\varphi_4$ are isomorphisms, $\varphi_1$ is surjective and $\varphi_5$ is injective, then $\varphi_3$ is an isomorphism (Stacks Lemma 12.5.20; Weibel Exercise 1.3.3 splits it into the two halves). In particular this holds when the four outer maps are isomorphisms.

blocks.caption: The ladder of the five lemma: two exact rows of five objects, joined by vertical maps making every square commute. If the second and fourth vertical maps are isomorphisms, the first is onto and the fifth is injective, the middle one is an isomorphism.
blocks.alt: Two rows, A1 to A2 to A3 to A4 to A5 on top and B1 to B2 to B3 to B4 to B5 below, with vertical arrows phi1 to phi5 from each A_i to B_i.
blocks.code:
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal, row sep=large]
A_1 \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "\varphi_1"] & A_2 \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "\varphi_2"] & A_3 \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "\varphi_3"] & A_4 \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "\varphi_4"] & A_5 \arrow[d, "\varphi_5"] \\
B_1 \arrow[r] & B_2 \arrow[r] & B_3 \arrow[r] & B_4 \arrow[r] & B_5
\end{tikzcd}

blocks.body:
Write $a_i\colon A_i\to A_{i+1}$ and $b_i\colon B_i\to B_{i+1}$.

Injectivity. Let $\varphi_3(x) = 0$. Then $\varphi_4a_3(x) = b_3\varphi_3(x) = 0$, so $a_3(x) = 0$ and $x = a_2(y)$. Now $b_2\varphi_2(y) = \varphi_3(x) = 0$, so $\varphi_2(y) = b_1(z)$; since $\varphi_1$ is onto, $z = \varphi_1(w)$, and $\varphi_2(a_1(w)) = b_1\varphi_1(w) = \varphi_2(y)$. As $\varphi_2$ is injective, $y = a_1(w)$ and $x = a_2a_1(w) = 0$.

Surjectivity. Let $u\in B_3$. Since $\varphi_4$ is onto, $b_3(u) = \varphi_4(v)$. Then $\varphi_5a_4(v) = b_4b_3(u) = 0$, so $a_4(v) = 0$ by injectivity of $\varphi_5$, and $v = a_3(x)$. Now $b_3(u-\varphi_3(x)) = b_3(u)-\varphi_4a_3(x) = 0$, so $u-\varphi_3(x) = b_2(s)$ with $s = \varphi_2(t)$. Then $u = \varphi_3(x+a_2(t))$.

blocks.title: The snake lemma for multiplication maps
blocks.body: Let $m,n\ge1$. Apply the snake lemma to multiplication by $m$ on each term of $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/n\to0$, and identify all six groups.
blocks.solution:
Multiplication by $m$ commutes with every homomorphism of abelian groups, so the diagram commutes. On $\mathbb{Z}$, multiplication by $m$ has kernel $0$ and cokernel $\mathbb{Z}/m$. On $\mathbb{Z}/n$ it has kernel $\{x: mx\equiv 0\}$, which is cyclic of order $d = \gcd(m,n)$, and cokernel $(\mathbb{Z}/n)/m(\mathbb{Z}/n) = \mathbb{Z}/(m,n) = \mathbb{Z}/d$. The rows are short exact, so the snake sequence extends by zeros:
$$0\to 0\to 0\to\mathbb{Z}/d\xrightarrow{\delta}\mathbb{Z}/m\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}/m\to\mathbb{Z}/d\to 0.$$
Exactness can be checked by hand: multiplication by $n$ on $\mathbb{Z}/m$ has kernel and cokernel of order $d$. Following the recipe, $\delta$ sends the generator $n/d$ of the kernel to the class of $m/d$: lift to $n/d\in\mathbb{Z}$, multiply by $m$, and divide by $n$. This pattern, the same group $\mathbb{Z}/\gcd(m,n)$ appearing as a kernel and a cokernel, is exactly $\mathrm{Tor}$ and $\mathrm{Ext}$ of cyclic groups (see [[tor]] and [[ext]]).

blocks.body:
1. Deduce from the snake lemma: if in a map of short exact sequences two of the three vertical maps are isomorphisms, so is the third.
2. Give an example of a commutative ladder of exact rows in which $\varphi_1,\varphi_2,\varphi_4,\varphi_5$ are non-zero but $\varphi_3$ is not an isomorphism; then one in which $A_3\cong B_3$ abstractly but no map $\varphi_3$ fills the ladder. (The five lemma needs a map.)
3. Prove the 'four lemma' halves separately: injectivity of $\varphi_3$ needs only $\varphi_2,\varphi_4$ injective and $\varphi_1$ surjective.
4. Let $u\colon M\to N$ and $v\colon N\to P$. Use the snake lemma on a suitable diagram to get an exact sequence
$$\begin{aligned}&0\to\ker u\to\ker vu\to\ker v\to{}\\ &\qquad\operatorname{coker}u\to\operatorname{coker}vu\to\operatorname{coker}v\to0.\end{aligned}$$

blocks.title: Complexes and the long exact sequence
blocks.body:
A chain complex $C_\bullet$ is a sequence of modules and maps $\cdots\to C_{n+1}\xrightarrow{d_{n+1}}C_n\xrightarrow{d_n}C_{n-1}\to\cdots$ with $d_nd_{n+1} = 0$; its homology is $H_n(C) = \ker d_n/\operatorname{im}d_{n+1}$, exactly as for the simplicial chain complexes on the [[homology]] page. A cochain complex has differentials raising degree, $d^n\colon C^n\to C^{n+1}$, and cohomology $H^n(C) = \ker d^n/\operatorname{im}d^{n-1}$. One passes between the two by $C^n = C_{-n}$, so every statement about one has a mirror image for the other. A complex is exact (or acyclic) if its homology vanishes everywhere.

A chain map $\varphi\colon C\to D$ is a family $\varphi_n\colon C_n\to D_n$ with $d\varphi = \varphi d$; it induces $H_n(\varphi)$ on homology, and $\varphi$ is a quasi-isomorphism if every $H_n(\varphi)$ is an isomorphism. Two chain maps $\varphi,\psi$ are chain homotopic if there are maps $s_n\colon C_n\to D_{n+1}$ with $\varphi-\psi = ds+sd$. Homotopic chain maps induce the same map on homology: if $z$ is a cycle then $\varphi(z)-\psi(z) = d(s z)+s(dz) = d(sz)$ is a boundary. Chain complexes of modules, with chain maps, form an abelian category in which kernels and cokernels are computed degreewise, so a sequence of complexes $0\to A_\bullet\to B_\bullet\to C_\bullet\to0$ is short exact when it is short exact in every degree.

The shift moves a complex one step and changes the sign of the differential; Weibel writes $C[p]_n = C_{n+p}$ with differential $(-1)^pd$, so $C[-1]_n = C_{n-1}$ (see the conventions below). The mapping cone of $\varphi\colon C\to D$ is the complex $\operatorname{cone}(\varphi)_n = C_{n-1}\oplus D_n$ with differential $(c,x)\mapsto(-dc,\ dx-\varphi(c))$, the sign used by Weibel (Definition 1.5.1) and Boe. One checks $d^2 = 0$ directly:
$$\begin{aligned}(c,x)&\mapsto(-dc,\ dx-\varphi c)\\ &\mapsto(ddc,\ ddx-d\varphi c+\varphi dc) = 0.\end{aligned}$$
The cone is used in the proof of the balancing theorem on [[derived-functors]].

blocks.title: Long exact homology sequence
blocks.body:
A short exact sequence of chain complexes $0\to A_\bullet\xrightarrow{f}B_\bullet\xrightarrow{g}C_\bullet\to0$ gives a long exact sequence
$$\begin{aligned}&\cdots\to H_n(A)\xrightarrow{f_*}H_n(B)\xrightarrow{g_*}H_n(C)\xrightarrow{\partial}{}\\ &\qquad H_{n-1}(A)\xrightarrow{f_*}H_{n-1}(B)\to\cdots,\end{aligned}$$
and the connecting maps $\partial$ are natural: a map of short exact sequences of complexes gives a commutative ladder of long exact sequences.

For a complex $X$ write $Z_n(X) = \ker d_n$ and $X_n/B_n(X) = \operatorname{coker}d_{n+1}$. The differential induces a map $\bar d\colon X_n/B_n(X)\to Z_{n-1}(X)$, with kernel $H_n(X)$ and cokernel $H_{n-1}(X)$.

Apply the snake lemma to the map of short exact rows given by $d$ on
$$0\to A_n\to B_n\to C_n\to 0\quad\text{and}$$
$$0\to A_{n-1}\to B_{n-1}\to C_{n-1}\to0.$$
Its kernels and cokernels give exact sequences $0\to Z_n(A)\to Z_n(B)\to Z_n(C)$ and
$$\begin{aligned}&A_{n-1}/B_{n-1}(A)\to B_{n-1}/B_{n-1}(B)\to{}\\ &\qquad C_{n-1}/B_{n-1}(C)\to0\end{aligned}$$
for every $n$. Shift the second by one degree and place the two as the rows of a new diagram, with top row
$$\begin{aligned}&A_n/B_n(A)\to B_n/B_n(B)\to{}\\ &\qquad C_n/B_n(C)\to0,\end{aligned}$$
bottom row
$$0\to Z_{n-1}(A)\to Z_{n-1}(B)\to Z_{n-1}(C),$$
and the three maps $\bar d$ from each term of the top row to the term below it as vertical maps. The squares commute because the maps of complexes commute with $d$. The snake lemma for this diagram is exactly
$$\begin{aligned}&H_n(A)\to H_n(B)\to H_n(C)\xrightarrow{\partial}{}\\ &\qquad H_{n-1}(A)\to H_{n-1}(B)\to H_{n-1}(C),\end{aligned}$$
and these six-term pieces overlap to form the long exact sequence. Unwinding the definition of $\delta$: for a cycle $c\in C_n$, lift to $b\in B_n$, apply $d$, and note $db$ lies in $A_{n-1}$; then $\partial[c] = [db]$. Naturality holds because each choice in this recipe can be transported along a map of short exact sequences.

blocks.title: Shifts and cones
blocks.body: Sources agree on the mathematics but not on the bookkeeping. Before reading a paper, check this one. (The indexing conventions for derived functors and double complexes are tabulated on [[derived-functors]], those for Ext on [[ext]].)

rows.text: For chain complexes $C[p]_n = C_{n+p}$ with differential $(-1)^pd$; the cone of $f\colon B\to C$ is $B_{n-1}\oplus C_n$ with $d(b,c) = (-db,\ dc-f(b))$. Other texts put $+f(b)$; this changes the cone only up to isomorphism, but signs in connecting maps must then be adjusted.

blocks.title: A long exact sequence computed by hand
blocks.body: Let $C$ be the complex $\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}$ in degrees $1, 0$, so $H_0(C) = \mathbb{Z}/2$, $H_1(C) = 0$. Tensor the short exact sequence $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$ with $C$ termwise (each $C_n$ is free, so the result is still short exact). Write out the long exact sequence and find the connecting map.
blocks.solution:
The three complexes are $C\xrightarrow{2}C\to C/2C$, where $C/2C$ is $\mathbb{Z}/2\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}/2$, with homology $\mathbb{Z}/2$ in degrees $1$ and $0$. The long exact sequence reads
$$0\to H_1(C)\xrightarrow{2}H_1(C)\to H_1(C/2C)\xrightarrow{\partial}H_0(C)\xrightarrow{2}H_0(C)\to H_0(C/2C)\to0,$$
that is, $0\to0\to0\to\mathbb{Z}/2\xrightarrow{\partial}\mathbb{Z}/2\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}/2\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$. Exactness forces $\partial$ to be an isomorphism. By the recipe: the generator of $H_1(C/2C)$ is the class of $1\in\mathbb{Z}/2$ in degree $1$; lift it to $1\in C_1 = \mathbb{Z}$; apply $d$ to get $2\in C_0$; this is $2$ times $1$, so $\partial$ sends it to $[1]\in H_0(C)$, the generator. The map $\partial$ is the Bockstein for this complex: it detects that the class in $H_0$ has order exactly $2$.

blocks.title: Splicing
blocks.body: If $A\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{g}C\xrightarrow{h}D\xrightarrow{k}E$ is exact, then $g$ and $h$ induce a short exact sequence $0\to\operatorname{coker}f\to C\to\ker k\to0$. This is how a long exact sequence is cut into short exact ones; it is used on [[tor]] in the proof of the Künneth formula and on [[ext]] to derive Anderson's sequence.

Since $gf = 0$, $g$ induces $\bar g\colon\operatorname{coker}f\to C$, injective because $\ker g = \operatorname{im}f$. Its image is $\operatorname{im}g = \ker h$. Finally $h$ maps $C$ onto $\operatorname{im}h = \ker k$.

1. Show that chain homotopy is an equivalence relation and is compatible with composition.
2. Verify that the mapping cone differential squares to zero, and that $0\to D\to\operatorname{cone}(\varphi)\to C[-1]\to0$ (with $C[-1]_n = C_{n-1}$ and differential $-d$) is a short exact sequence of complexes whose connecting map $H_n(C[-1]) = H_{n-1}(C)\to H_{n-1}(D)$ is $H_{n-1}(\varphi)$ (Weibel Lemma 1.5.3).
3. Deduce from Exercise 2 that $\varphi$ is a quasi-isomorphism if and only if its cone is exact.
4. Let $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ be short exact sequences of complexes, and suppose two of $A, B, C$ are exact. Show that the third is exact.

blocks.title: Resolutions and the comparison theorem
blocks.body:
A projective resolution of a module $A$ is an exact sequence
$$\cdots\to P_2\xrightarrow{d_2}P_1\xrightarrow{d_1}P_0\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}A\to0$$
with every $P_i$ projective; it is a free resolution if every $P_i$ is free. One usually writes it as $P_\bullet\to A$, meaning the complex $P_\bullet$ (with $P_i = 0$ for $i<0$) together with the augmentation $\varepsilon$; then $H_0(P_\bullet)\cong A$ and $H_i(P_\bullet) = 0$ for $i>0$. Dually, an injective resolution is an exact sequence $0\to B\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots$ with every $I^j$ injective.

Free resolutions always exist: map a free module $F_0$ onto $A$, then a free module $F_1$ onto the kernel $K_0 = \ker(F_0\to A)$, then onto $\ker(F_1\to K_0)$, and so on. The kernels $K_i$ are called syzygies. Injective resolutions exist by the dual procedure, using that modules have enough injectives. A resolution of length $n$ is one with $P_i = 0$ for $i>n$.

Over a PID, submodules of free modules are free, so every module has a free resolution $0\to F_1\to F_0\to A\to0$ of length one; this is why only $\mathrm{Tor}_1$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^1$ appear in topology over $\mathbb{Z}$. Over other rings resolutions can be forced to be infinite, as the next example shows. Resolutions are far from unique, and the key fact, which makes [[derived-functors]] well defined, is that any two are related by maps that are unique up to homotopy.

blocks.title: Four resolutions
blocks.body: Write down (a) a free resolution of $\mathbb{Z}/n$ over $\mathbb{Z}$; (b) an injective resolution of $\mathbb{Z}$ over $\mathbb{Z}$; (c) a free resolution of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ over $\mathbb{Z}/4$; (d) a free resolution of the trivial module $\mathbb{Z}$ over the group ring $\mathbb{Z}[C_n]$ of a cyclic group $C_n = \langle t\rangle$.
blocks.solution:
(a) $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/n\to0$.

(b) $0\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}\to0$, since $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ are divisible. In general an abelian group embeds in a divisible group whose quotient is again divisible, so injective resolutions over $\mathbb{Z}$ also have length one.

(c) Over $R = \mathbb{Z}/4$ the kernel of $R\to\mathbb{Z}/2$ is $2R\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$, the same module again. So the resolution never stops:
$$\cdots\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}/4\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}/4\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}/4\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0.$$
Exactness: the kernel and the image of multiplication by $2$ on $\mathbb{Z}/4$ are both $\{0,2\}$. Any projective resolution of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ over $\mathbb{Z}/4$ is infinite; this is shown in the section on homological dimension of [[ext]].

(d) In $\mathbb{Z}[C_n]$ let $N = 1+t+\cdots+t^{n-1}$. Then
$$\cdots\xrightarrow{N}\mathbb{Z}[C_n]\xrightarrow{t-1}\mathbb{Z}[C_n]\xrightarrow{N}\mathbb{Z}[C_n]\xrightarrow{t-1}\mathbb{Z}[C_n]\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}\mathbb{Z}\to0,$$
where $\varepsilon(t) = 1$, is exact. Indeed, writing $x = \sum a_it^i$, one has $(t-1)x = 0$ iff all $a_i$ are equal iff $x\in\mathbb{Z}N$, and $Nx = (\sum a_i)N = 0$ iff $\sum a_i = 0$ iff $x\in(t-1)\mathbb{Z}[C_n]$ (since $\ker\varepsilon$ is spanned by the $t^i-1$, which are multiples of $t-1$). This periodic resolution is the one Wikipedia gives for cyclic groups; it computes the cohomology of $C_n$ in the group cohomology section of [[ext]].

blocks.title: Comparison theorem
blocks.body: Let $P_\bullet\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}A$ be a complex of projective modules ($P_i = 0$ for $i<0$) with $\varepsilon d_1 = 0$, and let $Q_\bullet\xrightarrow{\eta}B$ be a resolution of $B$ (exact, but not necessarily projective). Then every homomorphism $f\colon A\to B$ lifts to a chain map $f_\bullet\colon P_\bullet\to Q_\bullet$ with $\eta f_0 = f\varepsilon$, and any two such lifts are chain homotopic (Weibel 2.2.6 and Porism 2.2.7, Boe Theorem 8.1.1). Dually, a map $B\to A$ lifts to a map from any coresolution of $B$ to a complex of injectives under $A$, uniquely up to homotopy (Weibel 2.3.7).

blocks.caption: The comparison theorem: a map f of modules lifts, one degree at a time, to a chain map between a complex of projectives over A and a resolution of B.
blocks.alt: Two rows: P2 to P1 to P0 to A to 0 and Q2 to Q1 to Q0 to B to 0, with dashed vertical arrows f2, f1, f0 and a solid vertical arrow f from A to B.
blocks.code:
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large]
\cdots \arrow[r] & P_2 \arrow[r, "d_2"] \arrow[d, dashed, "f_2"] & P_1 \arrow[r, "d_1"] \arrow[d, dashed, "f_1"] & P_0 \arrow[r, "\varepsilon"] \arrow[d, dashed, "f_0"] & A \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "f"] & 0 \\
\cdots \arrow[r] & Q_2 \arrow[r, "d_2'"] & Q_1 \arrow[r, "d_1'"] & Q_0 \arrow[r, "\eta"] & B \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}

blocks.body:
Existence. Since $\eta$ is onto and $P_0$ is projective, $f\varepsilon\colon P_0\to B$ lifts to $f_0\colon P_0\to Q_0$ with $\eta f_0 = f\varepsilon$. Suppose $f_0,\dots,f_n$ are built with $d'f_i = f_{i-1}d$ (and $\eta f_0 = f\varepsilon$). Then $f_nd_{n+1}$ maps $P_{n+1}$ into $\ker d'_n$ (into $\ker\eta$ when $n = 0$), because $d'_nf_nd_{n+1} = f_{n-1}d_nd_{n+1} = 0$. By exactness of $Q$, $\ker d'_n = \operatorname{im}d'_{n+1}$, so $d'_{n+1}\colon Q_{n+1}\to\ker d'_n$ is onto, and projectivity of $P_{n+1}$ gives $f_{n+1}$ with $d'_{n+1}f_{n+1} = f_nd_{n+1}$.

Uniqueness up to homotopy. By subtracting, it suffices to show that a lift $g_\bullet$ of $f = 0$ is null-homotopic, i.e. $g_n = d's_n+s_{n-1}d$ for maps $s_n\colon P_n\to Q_{n+1}$ (with $s_{-1} = 0$). Since $\eta g_0 = 0$, $g_0$ lands in $\ker\eta = \operatorname{im}d'_1$, so projectivity gives $s_0$ with $d'_1s_0 = g_0$. Suppose $s_0,\dots,s_{n-1}$ are built. Consider $h = g_n-s_{n-1}d_n$. Then
$$\begin{aligned}d'_nh &= d'_ng_n-d'_ns_{n-1}d_n\\ &= g_{n-1}d_n-(g_{n-1}-s_{n-2}d_{n-1})d_n\\ &= 0,\end{aligned}$$
so $h$ lands in $\ker d'_n = \operatorname{im}d'_{n+1}$, and projectivity gives $s_n$ with $d'_{n+1}s_n = h$, which is the required identity. Only projectivity of the $P_n$ and exactness of $Q$ were used. The dual statement has the dual proof.

blocks.title: Horseshoe lemma
blocks.body: Let $0\to A'\xrightarrow{i}A\xrightarrow{\pi}A''\to0$ be exact, and let $P'_\bullet\to A'$ and $P''_\bullet\to A''$ be projective resolutions. Then there is a projective resolution $P_\bullet\to A$ with $P_n = P'_n\oplus P''_n$ such that the inclusions and projections form a short exact sequence of complexes $0\to P'_\bullet\to P_\bullet\to P''_\bullet\to0$ lying over the given sequence. The dual statement holds for injective resolutions (Weibel 2.2.8, Boe Proposition 10.1.1).

Lift the augmentation $\varepsilon''\colon P''_0\to A''$ through the surjection $\pi$ to $\lambda\colon P''_0\to A$, using projectivity. Define $\varepsilon\colon P'_0\oplus P''_0\to A$ by $\varepsilon(x,y) = i\varepsilon'(x)+\lambda(y)$. The diagram with rows $0\to P'_0\to P'_0\oplus P''_0\to P''_0\to0$ and $0\to A'\to A\to A''\to0$ and vertical maps $\varepsilon',\varepsilon,\varepsilon''$ commutes. By the snake lemma, the kernels form an exact sequence $0\to K'_0\to K_0\to K''_0$ and $\operatorname{coker}\varepsilon$ sits between $\operatorname{coker}\varepsilon' = 0$ and $\operatorname{coker}\varepsilon'' = 0$, so $\varepsilon$ is onto; moreover the connecting map $K''_0\to\operatorname{coker}\varepsilon' = 0$ is zero, so $0\to K'_0\to K_0\to K''_0\to0$ is short exact. Now repeat the construction with this new short exact sequence of kernels and the resolutions $P'_{\ge1}\to K'_0$, $P''_{\ge1}\to K''_0$. Induction builds the whole resolution; each $P_n = P'_n\oplus P''_n$ is projective, and the rows are split exact in each degree (but the differential of $P$ is not the direct sum of the two differentials).

1. Find a free resolution of the abelian group with generators $x,y$ and relations $4x+6y = 0$, $6x+4y = 0$ (the group of the first example on the [[modules]] page).
2. Show that any two projective resolutions of $A$ are chain homotopy equivalent, by a homotopy equivalence lifting $\mathrm{id}_A$ that is unique up to homotopy.
3. Prove the injective version of the comparison theorem directly.
4. Find an injective resolution of $\mathbb{Z}/n$ over $\mathbb{Z}$ of length one.
5. Over $R = k[x]/(x^2)$, $k$ a field, find a free resolution of $k = R/(x)$ and show that every syzygy is isomorphic to $k$.

blocks.title: Reading the papers
blocks.body:
Here is where each paper's prerequisites from this page are treated; the rest of their homological algebra is on [[derived-functors]], [[tor]] and [[ext]].

1. Blanchette, Brüstle and Hanson, exact structures for persistence modules. Abelian categories and exact functors (exact sequences and abelian categories; exactness of Hom and tensor), projectives and their characterisation (the views on projective modules; the form through $\mathrm{Ext}^1$ is proved on [[ext]]).
2. Tang, profinite and solid cohomology. Enough projectives and enough injectives (the definition of that name), which decide which resolutions, and hence which derived functors, are available.
3. Bannister, derived limits in the Cohen model. The long exact sequence from the snake lemma (snake lemma), injectives, divisible groups and right adjoints of exact functors (Baer's criterion; enough projectives and enough injectives). Derived limits and $\delta$-functors are on [[derived-functors]].
4. Debray et al., the Smith fiber sequence. Long exact sequences as computational tools, and the five lemma, used in its Section 5.1 to see that a map of long exact sequences is an isomorphism (snake lemma and five lemma). Extension problems and Anderson duality are on [[ext]].

This page rests on [[modules]], [[categories-functors]] and the chain complexes of [[homology]]. Its resolutions and the comparison theorem are what make [[derived-functors]] well defined, and through them [[tor]] and [[ext]]; the horseshoe lemma gives their long exact sequences. The long exact homology sequence is used throughout [[cohomology]] of spaces, and [[spectral-sequences]] organise iterated long exact sequences. The diagram lemmas hold in any abelian category, including the sheaves of abelian groups behind [[sheaf-cohomology]], and group cohomology on [[ext]] leads to [[galois-cohomology]]. The adjunctions used for injectives (Hom-tensor, coinduction) are instances of [[yoneda-adjunctions]].

checks.claim: Snake lemma example: for multiplication by m on 0->Z-n->Z->Z/n->0 the six-term sequence 0->Z/d->Z/m-n->Z/m->Z/d->0 is exact (orders), and delta(n/d)=m/d
checks.python:
from math import gcd
for m in range(1,25):
    for n in range(1,25):
        d=gcd(m,n)
        # multiplication by n on Z/m: kernel and cokernel of order d
        ker=[x for x in range(m) if (n*x)%m==0]; img=set((n*x)%m for x in range(m))
        assert len(ker)==d and m//len(img)==d
        # delta: generator n/d of ker(m on Z/n) lifts to n/d in Z, times m = m*n/d = n*(m/d) -> class of m/d in Z/m
        assert (m*(n//d)) == n*(m//d)
        dl=(m//d)%m
        # delta injective with image = kernel of multiplication by n on Z/m
        image=set((k*dl)%m for k in range(d))
        assert image==set(ker) and len(image)==d

checks.claim: Mapping cone differential d(c,x) = (-dc, dx - phi c) squares to zero for a chain map (numerical check)
checks.python:
import sympy as sp
dc=sp.Matrix([[2,1],[0,3]])        # C_1 -> C_0
dd=sp.Matrix([[1,0],[1,1],[0,2]])  # D_1 = Z^2 -> D_0 = Z^3
phi1=sp.Matrix([[1,2],[0,1]])
phi0=dd*phi1*dc.inv()              # forces dd*phi1 = phi0*dc
assert dd*phi1==phi0*dc
# cone_2 = C_1, cone_1 = C_0 + D_1, cone_0 = D_0 ; d(c,x) = (-dc c, dd x - phi c)
D2=sp.Matrix.vstack(-dc, -phi1)          # C_1 -> C_0 + D_1
D1=sp.Matrix.hstack(-phi0, dd)           # C_0 + D_1 -> D_0
assert D1*D2==sp.zeros(3,2)

checks.claim: Splitting examples: s(y)=4y splits Z/6 -> Z/3 with Z/2 embedded as {0,3}; Z/4 has no section of reduction to Z/2; over Z/4 the map (2)->Z/2, 2->1 does not extend
checks.python:
assert all((4*y)%6%3==y for y in range(3)) and (4*3)%6==0
assert set((3*x)%6 for x in range(2))=={0,3} and set(v for v in range(6) if v%3==0)=={0,3}
# a section Z/2 -> Z/4 would send 1 to an element of order <=2 reducing to 1 mod 2
assert [v for v in range(4) if (2*v)%4==0 and v%2==1]==[]
# extension of (2)->Z/2 with 2->1 to Z/4: need x in Z/2 with 2x=1
assert [x for x in range(2) if (2*x)%2==1]==[]

checks.claim: Z/2 over Z/6 is projective (summand {0,3}) and injective by Baer's criterion; over Z/4 it is neither (Baer fails, and every order-2 element of (Z/4)^n is twice an element)
Exercise group <x,y | 4x+6y, 6x+4y> has a length-one free resolution Z^2 -> Z^2 (det -20 != 0) and is Z/2 + Z/10
checks.python:
import sympy as sp
from sympy.matrices.normalforms import smith_normal_form
A=sp.Matrix([[4,6],[6,4]]); assert A.det()==-20
S=smith_normal_form(A,domain=sp.ZZ); assert sorted(abs(S[i,i]) for i in range(2))==[2,10]
